papers.title: TideCache: Efficient Hybrid LLM Serving with Transparent Cache Management and Layer-Wise Streaming
papers.authors: Jinbin Luo, Xiaozhe Yao, Shang Yang, Zhijian Liu, Song Han, Qinghao Hu
papers.abstract: Hybrid architectures have become mainstream among open-weight language models. Their global-attention and bounded-state layers maintain heterogeneous caches whose demands vary with context length and concurrency. We present TideCache, a serving system on CPU--GPU superchips with three components for allocating GPU memory among caches and managing their residency across GPU and host memory. The Transparent Cache Pool redistributes physical pages among cache components behind fixed virtual addresses, preserving cache layouts and backend interfaces. The Cache Streamer uses computation intervals provided by bounded-state layers to prefetch the next global-attention layer's prefix into GPU slots shared across global-attention layers, reducing GPU residency while overlapping layer-wise transfers with computation. Generated KV remains resident. The Request Scheduler selects resident or streamed execution and triggers capacity adjustments according to request size and queue state. Together, they let HBM released by streaming accommodate other cache components and additional requests. Implemented in SGLang and evaluated on GB300 and GH200 across seven model/platform configurations, TideCache completes up to 2.04x as many agent turns, reduces overall P50 per-token latency by 20--59%, and improves agent P50 TTFT by 1.40--3.05x compared with SGLang with HiCache.
papers.summary: In hybrid LLMs, global-attention KV cache grows with both concurrency and context length, while bounded-state cache scales only with concurrency, so fixed GPU memory partitions can leave one pool underused while the other blocks requests. Hierarchical caching like HiCache keeps restored prefixes resident in GPU memory during decode, leaving the high-bandwidth CPU-GPU interconnect largely idle. Built in SGLang, TideCache keeps fixed virtual addresses for each cache subpool and remaps physical GPU pages on demand, shifting capacity across pools without changing cache layouts or attention backends. ==During decode, it uses bounded-state computation intervals to prefetch the next global-attention layer's host prefix into shared GPU slots==, keeping generated KV resident while the scheduler selects resident or streamed execution from request size and queue state. Across seven model and platform configurations on GB300 and GH200, it completes up to 2.04 times as many agent turns as SGLang with HiCache, cuts overall P50 per-token latency by 20% to 59%, and substantially improves agent P50 TTFT.

papers.title: Supercharging XLA-based inference: Announcing the launch of XLA Serving Engine
papers.summary: Many teams train models in Python, yet some production environments disallow Python and face interpreter and global interpreter lock overhead, so Google has open-sourced XLA Serving Engine for the OpenXLA ecosystem. It exports JAX models to an XLA SavedModel storing StableHLO computations and Orbax weights, then runs them in a native C++ runtime wrapping PJRT and the XLA compiler, supporting single-host and multi-host serving while preserving training kernel optimizations. In Google's short-request studies, it achieves 2 to 5 times the throughput of the best Python server they could build using a quarter of the memory. Internally, it already serves over 6 million queries per second across YouTube Shorts, Google Ads, Search, and parts of Gemini Omni. ==It is built as a lightweight one-shot inference engine typically for non-LLM models==, while the authors recommend vLLM or SGLang for large autoregressive language models with long contexts, and PyTorch export via TorchTPU is planned.

papers.title: E2E: Efficient Filtered AKNN Search via Adaptive Termination
papers.authors: Wenxuan Xia, Mingyu Yang, Wentao Li, Wei Wang
papers.abstract: Approximate k-Nearest Neighbor (AKNN) search is widely used in vector databases. When vectors carry additional attributes (e.g., labels or numerical values), filtered AKNN search retrieves the nearest vectors to a query vector under attribute constraints. Most existing methods use a fixed termination condition, searching the entire index while respecting attribute filters. However, this leads to substantial redundant computations, since different queries require different amounts of search effort, and thus misses early termination opportunities for easy queries. This paper proposes a lightweight model to estimate the search cost of filtered AKNN queries and enable adaptive termination : For easy queries, the search stops early to reduce latency, while for hard queries, it continues longer to preserve accuracy. The key challenge is accurate cost prediction under attribute filters. To address this, we show that information collected during an early probing phase (e.g., attribute distributions and intermediate distance statistics) can effectively predict the overall search cost. Experiments on six real-world datasets demonstrate 1.1× - 3.7× speedup over state-of-the-art baselines at 95% recall, while maintaining search accuracy.
papers.summary: In filtered approximate nearest neighbor search, graph indexes such as HNSW typically apply a fixed termination rule to every query, causing easy queries to explore far too many nodes. Early-termination models built for plain vector search look only at traversal distances and break down under filters, because ==when attributes and vector distances misalign, nearby nodes may still fail the filter==. During the mandatory early probing phase of graph search, E2E records the filter-matching ratios of visited nodes and queued candidates. It feeds both ratios and distance features into a lightweight LightGBM model to predict each query's computation budget, stopping easy queries early while letting hard ones search longer. In the high-recall regime, compared with Naive HNSW, it runs up to 2.6× faster on Tripclick and reduces distance computations by up to three times on YoutubeAudio, while improving efficiency by up to 1.5× when adapted to the filter-aware index ACORN. Without altering the underlying graph index, offline training on historical query logs cuts redundant traversal on easy filtered queries.

papers.title: RoCoKV: Accelerating LLM Inference Serving through Uncertainty and Redundancy Aware KV Cache Compression
papers.authors: Payman Behnam, Elaheh Sobhani, Saad Amin, Yahya Hassan, Daniyal Khan, Biswadeep Chakraborty, Tanish Patwa, Souvik Kundu, Alexey Tumanov
papers.abstract: KV cache compression is critical for large reasoning models, where most of the cost comes from long generated reasoning traces rather than the input prompt. These traces often contain redundant and low-utility tokens due to looping, self-verification, and corrections. However, such tokens may still receive high attention scores, making it difficult to remove them without harming the reasoning process. We propose RoCoKV, a KV cache compression method designed for large reasoning models. RoCoKV introduces two key components. First, uncertainty-guided adaptive pruning adjusts the compression strength based on the model's confidence, allocating more memory during uncertain phases and applying stronger pruning when the model is confident. Second, redundancy-aware token selection reduces the impact of tokens that are highly similar to recent reasoning content, encouraging the model to retain more informative and diverse tokens. Beyond the algorithm, we co-design RoCoKV with the serving stack: we develop fused three-phase CUDA decode kernels and integrate them into vLLM as a drop-in plugin that preserves its paged KV layout and CUDA graph capture, turning algorithmic savings into real end-to-end speedups. Extensive experiments across three reasoning benchmarks and two reasoning models demonstrate that RoCoKV consistently improves reasoning accuracy under constrained KV cache budgets, achieving higher accuracy compared to state-of-the-art KV cache compression methods. For DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B in vLLM, RoCoKV achieves a 1.27X speedup and 38% higher throughput on AIME25, the most challenging evaluated reasoning benchmark, and a 1.43X speedup and 45% higher throughput on the long synthetic benchmark, compared with Full-KV.
papers.summary: When large reasoning models generate long chains of thought, decode-stage KV cache compression depends heavily on timing. On AIME25, approximate attention token selection has little effect when output probabilities are concentrated, yet in uncertain steps with spread-out probabilities the flip rate of the most likely next token reaches 65%. Overly long generations with repetitive reasoning are also more likely to end in wrong answers. RoCoKV uses the entropy of the previous step's output distribution to adapt its budget without an extra forward pass, ==keeping more context during uncertain steps and pruning harder during confident ones==. It also uses a compact summary of recent context to down-weight repetitive tokens, avoiding full-cache pairwise comparisons. On the systems side, it plugs into vLLM with fused three-phase CUDA kernels that preserve paged KV cache management and CUDA graph execution, ==turning sparse compression into end-to-end speedups==. Across two reasoning models and three math benchmarks, it achieves higher accuracy than the evaluated compression baselines under tight budgets. Serving DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B on AIME25 in vLLM, it delivers a 1.27x speedup and 38% higher throughput than Full-KV.

papers.title: Berth: SLO-Preserving GPU Sharing Without New Preemption
papers.authors: Mohammadali Khodabandehlou, Mahdi Alizadeh, Lei Gao, Murali Annavaram, Bhaskar Krishnamachari
papers.abstract: Inference services keep GPUs reserved for their worst-case load, and most of that capacity sits idle. Filling it with best-effort work such as training is the obvious remedy, and latency is why it rarely happens: on a shared GPU, a request that must finish within milliseconds finds the best-effort job's kernels running or queued ahead of it. Spatial sharing cannot evict them, temporal sharing gives the request only its turn, and hardware partitioning protects it by idling what it does not use. Systems that keep both the SLO and the utilization have reached inside the stack (rewriting kernels, patching the driver, instrumenting the framework), which the operator of a closed GPU stack cannot do. This paper argues that reaching inside is unnecessary. The time-slicer built into commodity GPUs already preempts a running kernel within a fraction of a millisecond and switches the moment a context runs out of work; what it lacks is priority, and priority can be created from outside by controlling what the best-effort context has to run. Berth is a user-space system built on this observation: a preloaded shim feeds the best-effort job to the GPU only when no request needs it (feed control), a declared deadline reference extends the rule to continuous-batching LLM engines, and a shortened best-effort time slice, set without privileges, bounds what a long kernel can cost. Berth changes no application, framework, kernel or driver. Across 31 scenario points with MLPerf SLOs and 13 baselines, Berth meets SLOs within a few percentage points of running alone, above every baseline, with 2.7-3.5x the best-effort throughput of the strongest ones; beside LLM serving, it meets per-token targets for nearly every request while training keeps running. Sharing a closed GPU under SLOs needs no new preemption mechanism, only control over what the existing one sees.
papers.summary: Online inference GPUs sit largely idle off-peak, yet co-locating best-effort work such as training often breaks millisecond SLOs, and existing fixes either nearly halt the background job or rewrite kernels and patch drivers. This work shows that the stock time-slicer on commodity GPUs already preempts running kernels in under a millisecond; ==what it lacks is priority, which can be created in user space==. Berth is an unprivileged user-space system that leaves applications, frameworks, closed libraries, and drivers untouched. It holds best-effort kernel launches while a request is in flight, caps queued work during idle gaps, and shortens only the best-effort time slice to bound long kernels. Across MLPerf scenarios, Berth reaches 95.8% average SLO attainment, close to 97.9% alone, while keeping 48% of solo best-effort throughput, more than two and a half times what the closest baselines retain. For continuous-batching LLM serving, Berth feeds background work within each step's remaining slack, meeting per-token targets for nearly every request while training keeps running.

papers.title: TripleKV: Predict, Prefetch, Protect -- KV Cache Management for AI Agents
papers.authors: Shashwat Jaiswal, Chloe Alverti, Mengmei Ye, Chen Wang, Hubertus Franke, Fan Lai, Tianyin Xu, Josep Torrellas
papers.abstract: LLM agents alternate between inference and tool execution, repeatedly reusing their growing context across calls. Under high concurrency, their combined key-value (KV) cache working set can reach hundreds of GiB, far exceeding GPU memory capacity. As idle KV cache blocks are evicted to slower storage tiers, returning agents incur expensive retrievals that stall inference. > To address this problem, we present \emph{TripleKV}, a three-tier KV cache management system that hides the delays of these retrievals. %exploits tool execution to hide these delays. In agentic workloads, the KV blocks needed by the next inference request are known in advance; only the time of their reuse is uncertain. TripleKV uses a tool-aware latency predictor to estimate when each tool call will complete and prefetches the required KV blocks from SSD into host DRAM ahead of time. Unlike GPU prefetching, this avoids reserving scarce GPU memory and interfering with concurrent inference requests. To further improve DRAM utilization, TripleKV eliminates duplication of GPU-resident blocks in DRAM, and introduces a victim-cache mechanism that refills blocks from SSD upon their eviction from GPU memory. > Across data, web, and coding agents, TripleKV reduces the fraction of requests requiring critical-path SSD reads from 45--76\% to under 10\%. It also reduces P95 time to first token (TTFT) by up to 49\% compared with vLLM extended with DRAM and SSD KV-cache tiers, and achieves 1.5-7$\times$ lower P95 TTFT than recent agent-aware systems.
papers.summary: When multiple LLM agents run tool calls concurrently, idle KV cache blocks are quickly evicted from GPU memory and host DRAM, stalling returning requests for seconds on SSD reads. Pinning idle blocks in GPU memory or prefetching them straight to the GPU instead consumes scarce GPU capacity and lengthens queues. Because an agent's reused prefix is already known and only tool duration is uncertain, TripleKV predicts tool completion from tool type, input arguments, and live output cues, then prefetches the needed KV blocks from SSD into host DRAM. In DRAM, a multi-queue policy protects prefetched blocks from premature LRU eviction and removes duplicates of GPU-resident blocks. ==Prefetching into host DRAM instead of scarce GPU memory hides slow SSD reads without competing with active inference.== Across four agentic benchmarks, it cuts requests needing critical-path SSD reads from up to 76% to under 10%, lowers P95 TTFT by up to 49% over vLLM with DRAM and SSD tiers, and outperforms recent GPU-pinning and GPU-prefetching systems on tail latency and throughput.

papers.title: Twindex: Index Cache Offloading with Coarse-to-Fine Selection for Long-Context Sparse-Attention Serving
papers.authors: Yuxuan Xia, Jiakun Fan, Han Meng, Hao Mark Chen, Shenji Wan, Dongsheng Yang
papers.abstract: In long-context decoding, GPU memory (HBM) caps how many requests a GPU decodes at once. Sparse-attention models such as Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, DeepSeek V4.1-Flash and GLM-5.2 add an indexer: at every step it scores all past index entries with its own indexer cache, and attention reads the main KV of only the top-k entries. We find that once serving systems move the main KV to host memory, the indexer cache becomes the HBM bottleneck, at 63% of per-request HBM on Qwen and 75% on V4.1 at 1M tokens. Therefore, we introduce Twindex, which keeps only a compact copy of the indexer cache in HBM and the full indexer cache in host memory. At each step, the copy selects a larger candidate set, and the model's own indexer picks the top-k from the original rows of the candidates in host memory. The copy combines the shared component with the compressed residuals, both learned once offline. Twindex changes no model weights and runs inside CUDA graphs. At 1M tokens on modern GPUs, Twindex fits $1.78\times$, $1.62\times$ and $3.03\times$ as many requests as KV offloading alone on Qwen, V4.1 and GLM-5.2, and reaches $1.44\times$, $1.25\times$ and $2.54\times$ decode throughput when host memory does not limit the batch. Every request keeps its own index, and Qwen and GLM requests share prefix main KV in host memory. In our evaluations, mean benchmark scores are at most 3.1% below the baseline's.
papers.summary: During million-token decoding in sparse-attention models, even after offloading the main KV cache to host memory, the indexer cache left in GPU memory still caps concurrency, taking up to 90% of per-request HBM across the three tested Qwen, DeepSeek, and GLM models. Because the indexer scans every past entry at each step, direct PCIe offloading is too slow, while plain low-precision compression hurts recall. Twindex fits a shared cross-input position component offline and compresses only the residual, keeping compact keys and a hot buffer in HBM while storing full native rows in host memory. ==Each step screens a larger candidate set with compact keys, then rescores native rows with the original indexer for top-k==, without changing model weights and inside CUDA graphs. When host memory does not limit batch size and Qwen and GLM share prefix main KV, decode throughput across the three models reaches 1.25 to 2.54 times an optimized main-KV-offloading baseline, with mean benchmark scores at most 3.1% below baseline. Once the index shrinks, host memory can become the next concurrency bottleneck.

papers.title: Accelerating Mixture of Block Attention via Dynamic Routing, KV-Centric Execution and Runtime Pipelining
papers.authors: Yingqi Shi, Junru Lu, Yun Liu, Di Yin, Xing Sun
papers.abstract: Mixture of Block Attention (MoBA) reduces long-context computation by selecting key-value (KV) blocks for each query. FlashMoBA implements MoBA efficiently but retains a fixed Top-k budget and query-centric schedule. Fixed Top-k applies one budget across different score distributions and couples routing to task granularity; query-range ownership fragments K/V reuse when several ranges select the same column. We present LightningMoBA, which co-designs selection and execution through dynamic routing, KV-centric ownership, and runtime pipelining. Dynamic routing thresholds MoBA's per-query block scores and directly emits variable-cardinality sparse metadata. KV-centric ownership groups selected rows by (query head, KV block) column, splits high-fanout columns into bounded tasks, and reuses each task's loaded KV tile. On Hopper, pipelining overlaps regular K/V transfers and irregular query gathers with Tensor Core computation. Together, these mechanisms decouple retention from GPU scheduling granularity. At matched Top-16 retention across five checkpoints, LightningMoBA accelerates end-to-end generation by 1.20 to 1.60x while raising mean RULER score from 74.42 to 75.28.
papers.summary: In long-context block-sparse attention, giving every query a fixed block budget wastes work on weakly related blocks when scores are concentrated and drops relevant blocks when scores are diffuse. Assigning GPU work by query range also forces multiple thread blocks to reload the same KV block repeatedly. LightningMoBA keeps MoBA's mean-pooled block scoring and softmax computation, switching block selection to a per-query relative score threshold. It organizes execution around KV blocks, splits heavily selected blocks into row-capped subtasks, and uses Hopper GPU pipelining to overlap KV transfers, irregular query gathers, and matrix computation. Across five checkpoints on RULER at a matched Top-16 budget, it accelerates end-to-end generation by 1.20 to 1.60× over FlashMoBA. Mean RULER score rises from 74.42 to 75.28, though variable tracking drops across all five models at 64K context. Same-backend comparisons show execution optimizations drive most small-budget speedups, while at Top-64 dynamic routing yields simultaneous speed and accuracy gains on the evaluated models.

papers.title: Announcing distributed KV caching for self-hosted LLMs with Amazon ElastiCache
papers.authors: Meet Bhagdev, Chaitanya Nuthalapati, Kevin McGehee
papers.summary: When self-hosted LLM inference serves long-context multi-turn chats or document Q&A, single-server GPU and host memory KV caches are capacity-limited and local to one host, forcing prefill recomputation when requests route elsewhere, sessions return later, or a node fails. Amazon has launched fully managed distributed KV caching on ElastiCache for Valkey, adding a shared cache tier across GPUs in the same Availability Zone. Engines including vLLM, SGLang, and TensorRT-LLM connect via the open-source LMCache connector with only a configuration change, keeping hot blocks in DRAM, tiering colder blocks to local NVMe, and transferring KV state to GPU hosts via RDMA over EFA. ==Sharing KV state across servers frees fleets from pinning requests to one host and lets scaled-out or surviving servers reuse cached prefixes.== In shared-document Q&A tests, per-server requests per second doubled and cost per million output tokens dropped 40% after paying for the cache node. Across eight models, cache hits cut TTFT by 55% to 93%. Long-context reuse and retail or ads workloads with shared system prompts gain the most, and teams can run open-source KVTrace offline to estimate savings first.

papers.title: ECHO-2: A Large-Scale Distributed Rollout Framework for Cost-Efficient Reinforcement Learning
papers.authors: Jingwei Song, Meng Chen, Jie Xiao, Qingnan Ren, Jiaqi Huang, Yangshen Deng, Chris Tong, Wanyi Chen, Suli Wang, Zhisheng Chen, Ziqian Bi, Shuo Lu, Yiqun Duan, Xu Wang, Rymon Yu, Lynn Ai, Eric Yang, TIANYU SHI
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) is a critical stage in post-training large language models (LLMs), involving repeated interaction between rollout generation, reward evaluation, and centralized learning. Distributing rollout execution offers opportunities to leverage more cost-efficient inference resources, but introduces challenges in wide-area coordination and policy dissemination. We present ECHO-2, a distributed RL framework for post-training with remote inference workers and non-negligible dissemination latency. ECHO-2 combines centralized learning with distributed rollouts and treats bounded policy staleness as a user-controlled parameter, enabling rollout generation, dissemination, and training to overlap. We introduce an overlap-based capacity model that relates training time, dissemination latency, and rollout throughput, yielding a practical provisioning rule for sustaining learner utilization. To mitigate dissemination bottlenecks and lower cost, ECHO-2 employs peer-assisted pipelined broadcast and cost-aware activation of heterogeneous workers. Experiments on GRPO post-training of LLMs ranging from 4B to 32B parameters under real wide-area bandwidth regimes show that ECHO-2 significantly improves cost efficiency while preserving RL reward comparable to strong baselines.   3. 【5†2 Related Work】     1. 【6†2.1 Scoring, Granularity, and Budgeting in Sparse Attention】     2. 【7†2.2 Co-Design of Sparse Attention and Systems】     3. 【8†2.3 High-Performance Kernels on Modern GPUs】
papers.summary: During LLM RL post-training, rollout generation takes up most of the time, yet it usually shares expensive data-center GPUs with updates and often leaves the learner idle. ECHO-2 keeps centralized training on a small set of data-center GPUs and offloads rollouts to cheaper heterogeneous inference workers over a wide-area network. It treats policy staleness as a controllable budget so rollout generation, weight broadcast, and training overlap, activating the lowest-cost workers per unit throughput needed to saturate the learner. During broadcasts, workers form parallel peer-forwarding chains that relay chunks and switch to the new snapshot once installed, relieving the learner uplink bottleneck. In GRPO math post-training on Qwen3-8B over a wide-area network, it cuts cumulative cost by 33.3% to 36.3% over centralized baselines at matched AIME accuracy, with quality staying close to the synchronous baseline up to 6 steps of staleness. ==With bounded staleness and peer-forwarded broadcasts absorbing wide-area latency, cheaper distributed inference can take over rollout workloads without stalling training.==

scenario: Today's infrastructure track centers on caching, execution, and scheduling along the serving path, with KV cache at the core. Hybrid LLM serving pairs transparent cache management with layer-wise streaming, while another effort accelerates inference serving through uncertainty and redundancy aware KV cache compression. For AI agents, KV cache management focuses on prediction, prefetching, and protection, and self-hosted LLMs gain distributed KV caching with Amazon ElastiCache. Long-context serving keeps pushing into the runtime, as sparse-attention serving offloads index caches with coarse-to-fine selection and Mixture of Block Attention accelerates via dynamic routing, KV-centric execution, and runtime pipelining. XLA-based inference gains the dedicated XLA Serving Engine, and GPU sharing seeks to preserve SLOs without introducing new preemption. Filtered AKNN search speeds up with adaptive termination, while a large-scale distributed rollout framework targets cost-efficient reinforcement learning.
